---
title: "Ethics and transparency"
description: "Using data responsibly, and being open about how analysis informs decisions."
---

Analysis at NHSBSA uses data about people, and informs decisions that affect them. Two obligations
follow: use the data appropriately, and be open about how it was used.

## Data ethics

Analysis should be undertaken in line with legal and ethical obligations and any other relevant
public service codes of conduct.[^src-govs-010-principle-5]

The **Data and AI Ethics Framework** provides guidance on using data appropriately and responsibly
when planning, implementing and evaluating a policy or service.[^src-govs-010-section-6-1]

::: {.callout-note title="The framework was retitled and rescoped in December 2025" appearance="minimal" icon=false}
<br>
GovS 010 cites it as the **Data Ethics Framework**, which is the 2020 edition. On 18 December 2025 it
was retitled the **Data and AI Ethics Framework**, its scope was extended to AI and algorithmic
technologies, and four principles were added. Use the current framework, not the title GovS 010 names.

It publishes a **self-assessment tool**. Use that rather than a second instrument.
:::

Ethics is a design activity, not a compliance check at the end. The framework has seven principles,
and each one is a question worth asking before the work starts.

- **Transparency.** Could you explain to the people in the data what you did and why?
- **Accountability.** Who is answerable if this turns out to be wrong?
- **Fairness.** Could the analysis, or the decision it informs, affect some groups differently? Have
  you looked?
- **Privacy.** Is the data being used no more than the question requires? NHSBSA's Statistical
  Disclosure Control protocol and its Confidentiality and Access Statement are where this is already
  answered, and both are linked from [section 12](../12-tools-and-templates/index.qmd). Follow them
  rather than this page: a disclosure control protocol summarised in a playbook is a protocol with
  two versions.
- **Environmental sustainability.** What does producing and running this analysis cost, and is that
  proportionate to what it is for? This matters most for repeated pipelines and for anything using
  large models.
- **Societal impact.** Who is affected by the decision this analysis informs, beyond the people in
  the data? This is a scoping question, so it belongs in
  [section 4, phase 1](../04-analytical-lifecycle/index.qmd#phase-1-engagement-and-scoping) as well
  as here.
- **Safety.** What harm could follow if this is wrong, misread, or used for something it was not
  built for?

The last two are the ones with no established NHSBSA route. Societal impact in particular is worth
raising at scoping rather than discovering at publication.

Accountability is often the most clarifying of the seven. If nobody can answer it, the governance is
not yet in place. See [section 3](../03-roles-and-responsibilities/index.qmd).

## Personal data

Where personal data is used in analysis, this must be in accordance with NHSBSA policy and prevailing
legislation. That obligation comes from the legislation itself, not from this playbook and not from
GovS 010. The standard says the same in its own terms, that where personal data has been used this
should be in accordance with the organisation's policies and prevailing legislation.[^src-govs-010-section-6-14]

Where analysis using personal data is published, you may include in the publication:[^src-govs-010-section-6-14]

- when personal data has been used, and the justification for its use
- how guidance has been followed
- the steps taken to protect the data

Information and data should be classified and securely managed in line with GovS 007 Security, and
retained to meet statutory and contractual requirements and the requirements of the Data Ethics
Framework.[^src-govs-010-section-6-7]

**Ask before the work starts, not at sign-off.** Information governance advice, and the corporate
data protection impact assessment process, sit with the information governance function, and
[section 13](../13-getting-help/index.qmd) is the route to them. Go there while the question is
still what data to use, because a data protection impact assessment raised after the analysis is
built is a review of a decision already taken.

This playbook does not restate the DPIA process. It is a corporate process that applies to more than
analysis, and a second version of it here would go stale the first time it changed.

## Algorithmic transparency

Where an algorithmic tool informs a decision affecting the public, an **Algorithm Transparency
Recording Standard** entry is required.

The standard exists because a decision a person cannot interrogate is a decision they cannot
challenge. Publishing how a tool works, what data it uses and what it is for is what makes challenge
possible.

An entry typically covers what the tool does, why it is used, what data it was built on, how it
affects decisions, who is accountable for it, and what oversight it has.

::: {.callout-important title="If you cannot explain it, say so" appearance="minimal" icon=false}
<br>
Explainability is an assurance requirement, not a nice-to-have.

Where a method cannot be explained, for example a vendor-supplied scoring tool whose weighting is not
disclosed, **that limitation must be stated in the output** and an Algorithm Transparency Recording
Standard entry published.

"We can describe what goes in and what comes out but not how it works" is a finding about the
analysis, and the reader needs it.
:::

The same structured approach to business risk applies to black-box models as to any other. The
difficulty is in transparency, in having the right mix of experts available, and in understanding
what mitigations are possible. It is not a reason to assure them less.

**Who does what.** The analyst drafts the record as part of delivery, and the Head of Profession for
Statistics owns submission. The trigger is the Level 3 and Level 4 row in
[section 6](../06-doing-the-work/index.qmd) rather than a separate decision to be remembered, so an
analyst who is following their level is already doing it.

## Putting figures into the public domain

The Code of Practice for Statistics sets out **intelligent transparency**: taking an open, clear
and accessible approach to the use of data, statistics and wider analysis in the public domain, as
the default rather than as a decision to be made each time.

{{< include /guidance/_partials/diagram-public-domain.qmd >}}

**It binds more than official statistics.** The Code's Standards for the Public Use of Statistics,
Data and Wider Analysis apply to public bodies using statistics, data and wider analysis in the
public domain, and to everyone involved in that use rather than to analysts alone. A figure quoted
in a press release, a board paper made public, or a number given to a journalist is in scope. There
are three standards.[^src-code-of-practice-for-statistics-edition-3-0-standards-for-the-public-use-of-statistics-data-and-wider-analysis]

**1. Equality of access.** Make what is used in the public domain available to everyone in a timely
way, so the public can access, scrutinise and verify the claims made from it.

- draw on the latest and most reliable published official statistics where possible
- publish the figures **in advance of, or at the same time as**, their use in public communications
- publish them **separately from** any related policy or ministerial statement
- if unpublished figures are referred to publicly, publish them as soon as possible, ideally the
  same day

**2. Supporting understanding.** Use figures with integrity and communicate them with clarity and
accuracy, so the public can understand the basis for the claims made.

- do not cherry-pick figures, take them out of context, or place undue certainty on them
- communicate the key context and limitations alongside them
- be clear where the figures came from, citing sources in publications and on social media
- take proactive steps to prevent or minimise misinterpretation and misuse

**3. Decision making and leadership.** Seek and use impartial, expert advice when using figures in
the public domain.

::: {.callout-important title="The one that catches people out" appearance="minimal" icon=false}
<br>
Quoting an unpublished number in public starts a clock. Under equality of access it should be
published as soon as possible, ideally the same day, because until it is published nobody can check
the claim made from it.

If an analysis is going to be quoted before it is published, that is a conversation to have while
the analysis is being scoped, not after the quotation appears.
:::

## Transparency of the analysis itself

Beyond algorithmic tools, transparency means the ordinary discipline of being open about how a
result was reached:

- the assurance level applied, and why. See
  [section 5](../05-deciding-your-assurance-level/index.qmd)
- the quality assurance statement. See
  [section 9](../09-communicating-analysis/index.qmd)
- the data sources, extract dates and known quality issues
- the code, published where it can be

For official statistics, Standard 4 of the Code of Practice requires producers to manage data safely
and securely and be open about how it will be used and protected. Standard 1 requires them to
challenge misuse. See [section 2](../02-standards-landscape/index.qmd).
